**Monday, August 24, 1931**

You entered the world on a Monday in one of the most turbulent years of the twentieth century, at the very depth of the Great Depression. The breadlines were long, unemployment in the United States had climbed past 15 percent and was still rising, and governments across the Western world were lurching from crisis to crisis. The question hanging over 1931 wasn't whether the economic order would bend — it was whether it would break entirely.

---

**The day itself held a political earthquake across the Atlantic.** On August 24, 1931 — the precise day of your birth — British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's Labour government collapsed. Facing a catastrophic budget deficit and a run on the pound, the cabinet could not agree on spending cuts. MacDonald walked to Buckingham Palace, submitted his resignation, and was immediately asked by King George V to stay on and form a cross-party National Government to manage the emergency. It was one of the most dramatic single-day political reversals in British history: the man who had spent his career leading the Labour movement ended the day leading a coalition dominated by his opponents. You were born into a world where even stable democracies were improvising desperately.

---

**Your birth date shares something with one of history's most famous disasters.** On August 24 in the year 79 AD — 1,852 years before your birthday — Mount Vesuvius erupted, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum in ash and preserving them, accidentally, for future centuries to excavate. That date became synonymous with sudden, total catastrophe. There's something fitting about sharing it with a year when much of the world felt similarly buried.

---

**The world you were born into had no television.** Commercial broadcasting barely existed. Radio was the new and thrilling medium — families gathered around a single set. The Empire State Building, completed just three months before your birth in May 1931, was the tallest structure on earth. Long-distance telephone calls were exotic events. The first talking picture had arrived only four years earlier. The world was large in ways that are now almost unimaginable.

---

**Yet the transformation already underway was ferocious.** The previous decade had brought the automobile into mass use, electrified millions of homes, and made jazz and film global phenomena. The 1920s had felt like the future arriving all at once. Then came the crash of 1929, and by the August of your birth, that future was in question. The child born that Monday would spend their childhood watching the pieces get reassembled — slowly, painfully, and then, with the forced urgency of a world war, with extraordinary speed.

---

**Within ±30 days — a fuse being lit, 25 days later:** On September 18, 1931 — when you were just 25 days old — Japanese officers staged an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway and used it as a pretext to invade Manchuria. The Mukden Incident, as it came to be called, was a turning point in modern history: it was the first major act of aggression by a major power in the post-WWI order, it demonstrated that the League of Nations was toothless, and it set Japan on the path of expansion that would eventually draw the entire Pacific into war. The baby sleeping through late August had no idea that the fuse had just been lit.

---

**The lifetime that followed spans almost everything.** You were old enough to understand the Second World War — to feel its weight as a child, to know what was at stake. You came of age in the extraordinary postwar boom, a period of rising prosperity and technological confidence unlike anything the world had seen. At 38, you watched Neil Armstrong step onto the Moon. At 58, you watched the Berlin Wall come down. In your seventies, the internet rewired human communication. In your eighties, a small glass rectangle in your pocket connected you to virtually all recorded human knowledge. You have now lived into a world of artificial intelligence capable of writing coherent text and generating images from words — technologies that would have seemed like pure science fiction to the child born in the Depression.

---

You arrived in a world of breadlines, crackling radios, and genuine uncertainty about whether liberal democracy would survive the decade. You are 95 years old in a world that would be entirely unrecognizable to the people who celebrated your birth. That gap — between the Monday morning in August 1931 and today — is one of the most compressed and consequential stretches in human history. You have lived all of it.
